title: The pulley
hook: God gives people every gift but rest, so they'll come home (The Pulley)
tomorrow: what is prayer? Herbert answers with a list. how does it end?

segments.voice: Yesterday: so I did sit and eat, Herbert's guest at the table at last. Today, the same poet on why it's so hard to sit still.
screen: `SO I DID SIT AND EAT.` → `WHY IS SITTING STILL SO HARD?`

segments.voice: A day off, and somehow the to-do list grew. Herbert's poem The Pulley tells a story to explain it. When God first made man, a glass of blessings stood by. Let us pour on him all we can, God says. In flow strength, beauty, wisdom, honor, pleasure. Then God stops, with one gift left at the bottom of the glass: rest.
screen: `THE DAY OFF THAT FILLED UP.` → `A GLASS OF BLESSINGS.` → `ONE GIFT LEFT: REST.`

segments.voice: Why hold it back? Herbert gives God the reason: if I gave him this jewel too, "He would adore my gifts instead of me, And rest in Nature, not the God of Nature." So people get everything else, plus a restlessness that won't settle. "Let him be rich and weary, that at least, If goodness lead him not, yet weariness May toss him to my breast." That's the pulley: the weight that lifts you by pulling down. The teaching underneath is Christian: human restlessness has a direction, and rest is finally found in God. Jesus says it plainly in Matthew: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christians who keep Sunday, the Lord's Day, for worship and rest hear the same thing each week: rest is a gift, not a prize. Herbert's twist is gentle. In his story, the restless feeling isn't a failure. It's a rope God left in a person's hand.
screen: `THE GLASS OF BLESSINGS.` · `REST HELD BACK.` · `RICH AND WEARY.` · `COME UNTO ME: I WILL GIVE REST.` · then, large: `RESTLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Rest for the length of the sit. Close your eyes and let your hands go heavy in your lap. When the list starts talking, notice the pull toward doing and let it pull, without getting up. Herbert would call that pull the pulley.
The pulley: Herbert's picture of a restlessness that draws a person home.
For the road: restlessness, in Herbert's poem the gift held back so people would come looking. Day nineteen of twenty-one.

howItsDone: Many Christians keep Sunday, the Lord's Day, for worship and rest, and pray with Jesus' words in Matthew 11:28. Herbert's The Pulley is read as a story of why that rest can't be bought.
